# Devadūta Sutta (MN 130 (PTS MN iii 178))

**ID:** MN 130 (PTS MN iii 178)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Devadūta Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Messengers of the Gods
**PTS:** MN iii 178
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn130

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Devadūta Sutta* (MN 130) is a canonical discourse in the Majjhimanikāya, placed immediately after the *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta* (MN 129), with which it forms a pair of early Buddhist cosmographies of hell (*niraya*) [Marino 2017; SuttaCentral]. Expanding on the preceding discourse, it presents one of the canon's most elaborate and graphic descriptions of the netherworld [SuttaCentral; Trung Huynh 2016]. In the narrative, hell-guardians (*nirayapālā*) seize a deceased wrongdoer and drag him before King Yama, the ruler and judge of the underworld [Thich Thien Chau 1996; Cuevas 2008]. Yama interrogates the sinner on whether he noticed the divine messengers (*devadūta*)—manifestations of human vulnerability such as infancy, old age, sickness, punishment, and death—which serve as urgent reminders to practice wholesome conduct [Anālayo 2014; Cuevas 2008; Buddhist Forum 1994–96]. When the sinner confesses his heedlessness, Yama admonishes him that he alone is responsible for his unwholesome deeds, before remanding him to horrific underworld punishments, including tortures known by name such as *Rāhumukha* [Cuevas 2008; Buddhist Forum 1994–96; Marino 2017].

Curated parallels and DharmaNexus alignments demonstrate extensive textual reuse across Buddhist traditions. The sutta shares large textual blocks with its shorter counterpart in the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 3.36, sharing §7.12–17.1) and the preceding *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta* (§10.1–14.1) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Marino 2017; Thich Thien Chau 1996]. Extensive descriptions of the infernal torments are also shared with the *Niddesa* (Mnd 15, Cnd 23) and the *Kathāvatthu* (*Nirayapālakathā*, Kv 20.3) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Parallels in the Chinese Āgamas include MĀ 64 (T 26), EĀ 32.4 (T 125), and DĀ 30 (T 1), alongside independently transmitted translations such as T 42, T 43 (*Yanluo wang wu tianshizhe jing*), and T 86 (*Tiecheng nili jing*) [SuttaCentral; Marino 2017; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus further records alignments with the Tibetan *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthānasūtra* (D0287) and Sanskrit works such as the *Mahāvastu Avadāna* and *Saṃghāṭa Sūtra* [DharmaNexus].

In exegesis and Buddhist history, the commentary clarifies esoteric names of punishments, glossing *Rāhumukha* as the practice of propping open the condemned person's mouth with a peg and lighting a lamp inside [Marino 2017]. Traditional chronicles also cite the sutta as an instrument of early Buddhist conversion: Mahinda is recorded as reciting the *Devadūta Suttanta* in Sri Lanka [Adikaram 1946], while the missionary Mahādeva is said to have preached it to convert Mahiṣamaṇḍala [Buswell & Lopez 2014]. Modern English translations include those by Bhikkhu Bodhi and Bhikkhu Sujato [Cuevas 2008; SuttaCentral].
